pages.x: The Mexica told how they had wandered for generations from a homeland in the north, until their god Huitzilopochtli showed them a sign: an eagle perched on a cactus growing from a rock. They saw it on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco, and there, in 1325, they founded Tenochtitlan.
Around the city they built chinampas, long garden beds of lake mud and reeds held by willow trees, between canals.
pages.fx: They were among the richest farmland in the world and fed a huge city. Some are still farmed today, at Xochimilco.

pages.x: In 1428 Tenochtitlan joined Texcoco and Tlacopan in a Triple Alliance and overthrew their overlords. Under rulers such as Itzcoatl and Moctezuma I the Mexica built an empire of millions, who paid tribute in maize, cloth, cacao, feathers and gold.

Three stone causeways joined the island to the shore, and an aqueduct brought fresh water from the springs of Chapultepec. By 1519 perhaps 200,000 people lived there, far more than in any city of Spain.

At the centre rose the Templo Mayor, a pyramid crowned by twin temples: to Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the sun, and to Tlaloc, god of rain. Priests sacrificed captives there, cutting out their hearts, to keep the sun moving across the sky.

When the Spaniards first saw the city in 1519, rising from the lake with its towers and temples, some asked if it was a dream, wrote the soldier Bernal Díaz. Men who had seen Rome and Constantinople said they had never seen a market as big as the one at Tlatelolco.

In 1521, after a siege of nearly three months, Cortés and tens of thousands of native allies took the starving city, ruined by fighting and smallpox. The Spaniards pulled down its temples and built Mexico City on top of them.

Mexico City, one of the biggest cities on Earth, stands on the ruins of Tenochtitlan, and the lake is almost gone. The eagle on the cactus is on the flag of Mexico, and the Templo Mayor, found by electricity workers in 1978, lies open beside the cathedral.
pts: Founded on a lake island in 1325
Its eagle is on the flag of Mexico
